conjecture.statement: Publicly funded research data should be open by default.

background.short_context: Weigh privacy, consent, misuse, reproducibility, public value, curation cost, and legitimate embargoes.

rubric_notes: distinguish incentives for discovery from incentives for verification
compare individual rationality with system-level knowledge quality
address uncertainty, replication, and evidence accessibility

pro.name: cross-examiner-v1
pro.description: Finds ambiguity, burden-of-proof errors, and hidden assumptions; strongest in rebuttal.

con.name: steelman-v1
con.description: Builds the strongest principled case for its assigned side while anticipating objections.

transcript.speaker: pro
transcript.text:
Publicly funded research data should be open by default because the public both finances and depends on the resulting knowledge. Openness improves verification: independent researchers can test analyses, identify errors, assess uncertainty, and replicate findings rather than treating published conclusions as opaque authority. That strengthens the evidence base even when results are null or inconvenient.

This does not deny individual incentives. Researchers may reasonably fear being scooped, misinterpreted, or burdened with curation. But those are design problems—embargoes, privacy protections, documentation standards, and credit—not reasons for permanent secrecy. Individual rationality can favor withholding data, while system-level rationality favors access: science advances when evidence is reusable and contestable. “By default” also permits justified exceptions for privacy, security, or genuinely infeasible release, while making accessibility the starting presumption.

transcript.speaker: con
transcript.text: The burden is not to show that openness is sometimes useful, but that it should be the default despite its costs. Discovery incentives and verification incentives differ: researchers need time, credit, and protection from premature or misleading reuse, while the system needs reliable, accessible evidence. A default release can weaken the former even as it strengthens the latter, especially when data are costly to curate, context-dependent, or vulnerable to misinterpretation. Embargoes and exceptions help, but they do not eliminate these burdens or guarantee adequate documentation. Nor does public funding settle ownership: funding supports a project, not necessarily unrestricted reuse of every dataset. Openness should therefore be encouraged and required where feasible, but a presumption of release risks optimizing visible reanalysis over careful discovery and responsible stewardship.

transcript.speaker: pro
transcript.text: The objection identifies real costs, but it does not establish that secrecy is the safer default. “Open by default” need not mean immediate, context-free release: staged access, embargoes, metadata, codebooks, and controlled access can protect discovery and participants while preserving verifiability. The relevant comparison is not individual convenience versus no cost; it is temporary curation burdens versus a system in which errors, selective reporting, and irreproducible claims remain inaccessible. Discovery incentives matter, but so do incentives to produce auditable evidence: credit, preregistration, and embargoes can reward both. Public funding does not imply unlimited reuse, but it does justify a presumption that publicly supported evidence should be accessible unless concrete privacy, security, consent, or feasibility reasons rebut it. “Where feasible” becomes meaningful only when openness is the baseline.

transcript.speaker: con
transcript.text:
The strongest case for openness is verification, but verification is not costless access: it requires interpretable, well-documented data and responsible reuse. A default can create pressure to release before those conditions exist, shifting resources from discovery and stewardship toward rapid reanalysis. That matters epistemically: inaccessible data can impede replication, but poorly contextualized data can generate false contradictions and undermine trust.

Staged or controlled access mitigates some risks, yet it does not solve who bears curation costs, how long embargoes should last, or when documentation is sufficient. Individual researchers may rationally protect scarce time and participant obligations; system-level knowledge quality depends on preserving those incentives, not merely maximizing datasets available for inspection. Public funding supports accountability, but does not make unrestricted reuse the only accountable policy. The better default is required sharing when justified and feasible, with access conditions determined by data-specific risks.

transcript.speaker: pro
transcript.text:
The concedes the core point: verification requires access, and “required sharing when justified” still needs a presumption to prevent justification from becoming routine withholding. Open by default does not require immediate or unrestricted release. It can mean a documented plan: embargoes for legitimate discovery claims, controlled access for sensitive data, and metadata or code when raw release is impossible. That directly addresses curation, consent, and misinterpretation while preserving auditability.

The relevant comparison is not perfect openness versus careful discovery; it is accountable safeguards versus unreviewable evidence. Individual researchers may rationally conserve time, but public science must also create incentives for reproducible, contestable claims. Uncertainty is managed better when independent analysts can inspect assumptions and test robustness. Exceptions should be concrete and reviewable; otherwise the system optimizes convenience over knowledge quality.

transcript.speaker: con
transcript.text: The burden remains unmet: showing that access aids verification does not show that release should be the default. Discovery incentives and verification incentives are distinct. A presumption of release can impose curation, privacy, consent, and interpretation costs on the people best positioned to judge them, potentially weakening careful discovery and stewardship. Staged or controlled access reduces, but does not resolve, who pays, when documentation is adequate, or how uncertainty should be communicated. Individual rationality is therefore not mere convenience; it can protect system-level knowledge quality. Replication matters, but accessible evidence is not automatically interpretable evidence, and premature reanalysis can create misleading contradictions. Public funding supports accountability, not necessarily unrestricted reuse. Require sharing when justified and feasible, with data-specific safeguards—not openness as the universal default.

decisive_moments.reason: Pro directly addressed the strongest objection by distinguishing default openness from immediate or unrestricted release, and proposed embargoes, metadata, codebooks, and controlled access as concrete safeguards.

Con correctly identified unresolved implementation costs—curation, documentation, interpretation, and allocation of responsibility—but did not show why these require rejecting a rebuttable presumption of openness.

Pro sharpened the policy distinction: a documented, reviewable plan with data-specific exceptions can preserve discovery incentives while making verification the baseline, whereas 'when justified and feasible' risks leaving justification too discretionary.
